A sysadmin deployed Gitea as a Git server for an 8-user project. It was much simpler than a full GitLab instance: one binary to run. Users were instantly familiar with the GitHub-like interface, and non-contributors read source through the web UI instead of cloning.

A devops sysadmin who started with GitLab wishes they had chosen Gogs/Gitea. Gitea is 'massively less resource hungry,' whereas their GitLab install uses 4 cores, 8GB RAM and 2.3TB of disk, and its backup rake task triggered the OOM killer three times.

Runs Gitea on a $5 VPS for all personal projects and says it works great, good enough for ~80% of use cases. They access the UI over an SSH port-forward because they're unsure how secure it is exposed publicly. Wants a GitHub Pages-like static site feature behind the Gitea login.

Gitea supports OAuth2, which Gogs dropped, and has other useful features over Gogs. Gitea focuses on Git hosting rather than bundling CI and chat like GitLab; you connect other tools only if you need them.
After browsing the Gitea test instance, a commenter found it grating due to UX, CSS, design, spacing and typeface issues they see as common in open source software.

Uses Gitea (previously Gogs) for a team of 45 with a very pleasant experience. Docker setup was smooth and works easily with Certbot. Downside: a lack of good documentation, so they fall back on Gogs' docs.
'That was a painless installation.' The commenter says other self-hosted projects should imitate it, noting they skipped Discourse, Mastodon and GitLab because those were painful to set up.
Has used Gitea + Drone for several years and 'couldn't be happier': stable, fast, and it just works without consuming lots of RAM.
Gitea can also act as an OIDC identity provider, making it handy as the linchpin for SSO across a set of developer services.
Last time they tried Gitea, migrating existing git repos was surprisingly difficult.
Has used it 4+ years with no complaints, and it keeps getting better. Each upgrade is super simple: stop the service, replace the single binary, start it.

A startup using Gitea says it needs a lot of improvement. They cite migrations that go up but not down, a nonstandard web framework (go-macaron), too much logic in Go templates, and strange error reporting. 'Gitea isn't a great Go codebase,' though much was inherited from Gogs.
Has used Gitea for years; being written in Go makes it easy to run from a USB stick. The mirror feature keeps local copies of followed projects and saved them when authors deleted repos.
Migrated the TiDB repo to the 'Try Gitea' service and found the Activity tab very slow: a 1-year period took nearly 90s to load. Re-selecting it took the same time, suggesting no caching.
Painless only to a point: fine for a one-person show or small company, but as you get bigger you hit various issues often and wish for GitHub again.
Sorely misses subscription/watch management, e.g. listing and filtering watched items by repo, author, type or reason as on GitHub. There is also no user-facing session management.

Moved from self-hosted GitLab to Gitea + Nexus + Drone because keeping GitLab updated was cumbersome. They find GitHub/GitLab UI better for organization and group navigation. On 4GB RAM, Gitea is far more performant: the difference between a snappy and an annoyingly laggy UI.

Complaint about breakages in 1.17, such as newly reserved usernames. They also cite a PR adding regex email validation that pushed ahead despite reviewer objections, while a related issue remains open.

Gitea performs well even on slow hardware (a fitlet2 with an Atom x7-E3950 and 16GB RAM), whereas GitLab, which they use at work, doesn't. Another user says the 1.17 package registry lets them ditch Verdaccio.
Asks whether Gitea still lacks a good backup and restore mechanism, calling that a show stopper for moving off Gogs.
